lessons.title: hablé — the regular past, built on an accent
lessons.gloss: the regular -ar preterite — hablé, hablaste, habló — and why the accent matters

segments.text: Fui was irregular; now the pattern that covers thousands of verbs. Take any regular -ar verb, drop the -ar, and add the preterite endings. The whole tense hangs on one small mark: the accent.
accent-acute — the written ´ marks the stressed vowel: habl-É, habl-Ó. Say the stress at the very end and the past tense announces itself.
Drop -ar from hablar ("to speak") and add:

Compare it with the present you learned in Chapter 6 — hablo, hablas, habla — and the difference is almost entirely where the stress lands: HABlo (I speak, now) vs hablÉ (I spoke, done). The accent is not decoration; it carries the tense.

These endings are worn-down Latin perfect forms. Latin amāvī ("I loved") becomes amé; amāvistī becomes amaste; amāvit becomes amó. The -āv- dissolved and left the stressed final vowel that Spanish now crowns with an accent. So hablé is (fabulāvī) with the middle chewed away — the same erosion you've watched all along, applied to a whole tense.
hablamos is the same in present and preterite ("we speak" / "we spoke"). Only context — or a time-word like ayer ("yesterday") — tells them apart: hablamos ayer = "we spoke yesterday."

lessons.title: Practice — the preterite, past against present
lessons.gloss: past vs present — fui, hablé, and the forms that look the same

segments.text: This chapter gave you the past: the shared ser/ir preterite (fui) and the regular -ar pattern (hablé). Time to switch between now and then without stumbling.
fui (ser/ir): fui, fuiste, fue, fuimos, fueron.
hablé (regular -ar): hablé, hablaste, habló, hablamos, hablaron.

blocks.title: Drill 2 — the accent flips the tense

segments.text: Say each present form, then its preterite twin — the stress jumps to the end:
hablo (I speak) becomes hablé (I spoke).
habla (s/he speaks) becomes habló (s/he spoke).
trabajo (I work) becomes trabajé (I worked).
What one thing changed? (The accent — the stressed syllable moved to the end.)
For each fui/fue, say whether it's "to be" or "to go":
"Fui a la escuela." becomes? (ir — "I went.")
"Fui estudiante." becomes? (ser — "I was a student.")
"Ella fue muy amable." becomes? (ser — "She was very kind.")
"Ellos fueron a España." becomes? (ir — "They went.")
Say each out loud:
"Ayer hablé con mi madre." — "Yesterday I spoke with my mother."
"Fui al mercado y compré pan." — "I went to the market and bought bread."
"Fuimos amigos." — "We were friends."

Which two verbs share the preterite fui/fue? (ser and ir.) How does the accent change hablo into habló? (It moves the stress to the end — present becomes preterite.) In "Fui a casa," be/go? (Go — ir.) You can now speak in the past — the course has crossed from "what is" to "what happened."

lessons.title: fui — the past tense arrives, and two verbs become one
lessons.gloss: the preterite (past) — and the astonishing fact that "I was" and "I went" are the same word

segments.text: A big moment: your first past tense. Spanish's everyday past is the preterite — "I spoke, I went, I was." And it opens with the strangest, most memorable fact in the whole language: the verbs ser ("to be") and ir ("to go") have the exact same preterite. Fui means both "I was" and "I went."
stress-final — the preterite loves the final syllable: fui, fue (one-syllable), then fuiste, fuimos, fueron.
One set of forms, two verbs. There is no separate past for "to go" — Spanish just reuses "to be."

blocks.title: Why? A tale of two "be" verbs

segments.text: fui comes from Latin fuī, "I have been" — but here is the twist: Latin had two roots for "to be." The present sum/es/est ( becomes soy/eres/es) came from PIE es-; the perfect fuī came from a different root, PIE bʰuH-, "to grow, become" — the very root of English be, been, and (through Greek and Latin) future and physics. Spanish stitched the two roots into one verb — that's suppletion, like English go/went.
Then ir ("to go") borrowed fuī too, because Latin's own past of īre had worn away. So "to be" and "to go" merged in the past — and only context tells them apart:
Fui a Madrid. — "I went to Madrid." (movement becomes ir).
Fui profesor. — "I was a teacher." (state becomes ser).
